notes.meaning: Solomon points out a painful burden that rests heavily on human beings. He looks at life from an earthly viewpoint and sees a heartbreaking trouble that touches many people. Wealth and success do not automatically bring peace or happiness.

A person may receive riches, property, and honor from God, having everything anyone could wish for. Yet God does not give him the inner power or contentment to actually enjoy what he owns. Instead, an outsider or stranger ends up taking and enjoying his goods, leaving the rich man empty-handed.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern interpreters see this as showing that true human ownership is an illusion, because all material wealth remains entirely in God's hands to give or take away.

notes.meaning: In ancient times, having a large family and living a very long life were considered the greatest signs of God's blessing. Yet even if a man has a hundred children and lives for many years, his life is hollow if he never finds true joy and does not even receive an honorable burial. A baby who dies before birth is in a better state than an unsatisfied man who wastes his life.

A stillborn infant arrives without purpose and slips away in darkness, never receiving a known name in this world. It never sees the light of the sun and never learns of earthly troubles. Because it is spared the pain, sorrow, and bitter disappointment of a wasted life, it has more rest than the unhappy, greedy man.

Even if a man could live two thousand years, that long time would only be lengthened misery if he never enjoys true goodness. When life ends, both the long-lived man and the stillborn infant end up in the grave, the common resting place of all humanity. Length of days has no value on its own unless God grants peace and enjoyment with it.

People work hard day after day just to earn food to fill their mouths. Yet physical food can never satisfy the deep, inner cravings of the human soul. Our earthly work meets bodily needs for a moment, but our hearts remain restless without God.

In basic earthly needs, a wise person does not have any obvious advantage over a foolish person. Both must eat to live, and both face sickness, sorrow, and death. Even a humble poor man who knows how to behave properly in public faces the same human limits as anyone else.

It is far better to be content with the good things right before your eyes than to let your heart wander after things you do not have. Chasing endless desires only brings frustration, like trying to chase and catch the wind. Learning to enjoy present blessings brings quietness of soul.

Everything that exists has already been appointed and named by God, who set the limits of human life long ago. Man was made from the dust of the earth, and his name reminds him that he is weak and mortal. Because God is all-powerful, it is pointless and foolish for a frail human being to argue or dispute with Him.

The more people argue with God or pile up earthly possessions, the more they feel the emptiness of life. Words and debates cannot change human weakness or alter God's decrees. Talking back to the Creator never helps a person find true peace.

No mortal person truly knows what is best for himself in this life, which passes away as quickly as a shadow. Human beings cannot tell what will happen after they die or how their work will be handled under the sun. True wisdom means trusting our unknown future to God instead of worrying over things we cannot control.
